title: A supply choice in my Codex-built railway game had one obvious answer. Here’s what changed.
author: RobeertIV
selftext:
I'm the creator of Tickets for the Afterlight, a $3, in-development Windows puzzle adventure built in RPG Maker MV with OpenAI Codex and adapted Higgsfield artwork. AI also assisted/generated the dialogue, interface graphics, puzzle data and synthesized music scripts. This is captured gameplay from the game, using prepared progress saves to show several systems: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wTwAH24PuL4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wTwAH24PuL4)



An early version leaned too heavily on messages. Asking for more minigames increased the checklist, but did not answer why a player should care about the next repair. The 3.1 pass organizes the main route around station machinery and lets a supply choice change how later finale boards start. One allocation originally made every task easier; it was revised so each choice prepares different parts of the station. Two passenger requests now require physical puzzle actions as well.



The useful technical split was keeping puzzle state and legal actions separate from presentation, then checking saves and both branches in the actual MV runtime. Those checks establish that routes work, not that they are fun. No LLM runs while you play. The free demo covers twelve first-station repairs and six optional service boards: [https://robeertiv.itch.io/tickets-for-the-afterlight](https://robeertiv.itch.io/tickets-for-the-afterlight)



How do other AI-assisted game projects test whether a new system changes decisions rather than just adds content?
